What are social video metrics and why do they matter?

Social video metrics are the numbers that show how your video content performs on social media platforms. They track how often your videos are watched, how people interact with them, and what actions viewers take after watching.

At their best, video marketing metrics don’t just tell you what happened, they show you why. These are the insights that help shape smarter content, better social media campaigns, and a stronger connection with your target audience.
Some examples of social video metrics include:
View count: How many times your video was played.
Watch time: How long people stayed engaged.
Engagement rate: How often viewers interacted (likes, comments, shares).
Video completion rate: How many viewers watched all the way through.
Play rate: What share of people who saw your video actually pressed play.
Click-through rate (CTR): How often viewers clicked on your call-to-action (CTA).
Shares and saves: Indicators of content that resonates and drives social sharing.

These metrics matter because they’re how you measure the actual impact of your video strategy. They help you understand what’s working (and what’s not), refine your creative and messaging, and compare performance across social channels.

They also matter upward. When roughly $1 of every $5 in digital ads goes to social video, metrics are the bridge between creative work and business outcomes, especially when you need to defend video budget or justify headcount. A clean set of numbers tied to revenue, pipeline, or reach is what turns a quarterly report into buy-in. Pulling those numbers from social media analytics tools makes that reporting far less painful than stitching together screenshots from six dashboards.

Which social video metrics should you track?

The video metrics you should track depend entirely on your goals. For example, what you’d measure for a brand awareness campaign looks completely different from what you’d measure for a community-building one.
Before you dive into the full list, here’s the short version of how social media video KPIs map to common goals:
Awareness goals: Lean on reach-based metrics like views and impressions.
Attention goals: Lean on watch time, completion rate, and retention.
Revenue goals: Lean on CTR, conversion rate, and traffic source.
Here’s a fuller guide to which metrics to track based on your goal:
Average watch time, retention, video completion rate
Conversion rate, click-through rate, traffic source
Our advice? Pick two or three KPIs that align with your goal, and don’t get distracted by the rest.
11 top social video metrics to track (and why they matter)
Here are the top social video metrics that can tell you the most about your performance across all channels.

View count tells you how many times your video has been watched. But don’t let that simplicity fool you. Views are still one of the most important video metrics, especially for measuring brand awareness and reach.
Every platform defines a “view” differently, so context matters.
Here’s what counts as a view by platform:
Facebook:Reel: The moment the video starts playingIn-feed video: 3 seconds or more
Instagram:Reel: The moment the video starts playing (including replays)In-feed video: 3 seconds or more
YouTube:Video: 30 seconds or moreShorts: The moment your video starts playing. Note: this means even if a user scrolls past, it counts as a view as long as the video begins to play.
TikTok: 1 second (or 3 seconds for videos 3 minutes and longer)
LinkedIn: 2 seconds or more, with at least 50% of the video on screen
X (Twitter): 2 seconds or more, with at least 50% of the video on screen
Snapchat: 1 second or more for organic Stories (Snap Ads count a video view at 2 seconds)
“From an awareness standpoint, we care about how widely shared the video is to see if this was something the algorithm favored,” says Eileen Kwok, Former Social Media Strategist at Hootsuite.
Even the platforms themselves are leaning into views. Facebook made views the primary metric across reels, videos, posts, and stories, following the same approach Instagram adopted.

That said, views aren’t always what they seem. Some platforms, including Meta, have been called out for inflated video metrics. A 2018 lawsuit centered on overstated average viewing time figures. It’s a reminder that view count is a helpful signal, but not the whole story.

If your video views are consistent, you know your videos are regularly reaching people. Congrats! You’re in a pretty good position. But if they’re swinging up and down, take a closer look at your top performers to figure out what’s clicking.

Generally, social media engagement describes how your audience interacts with your content. Video engagement rate includes likes, comments, shares, and saves, and can indicate how much your video resonated with viewers.
People like Adam Mosseri, Head of Instagram, are pretty clear that engagement metrics are among the most important to track.
You can review these social media metrics in the platforms themselves, or you can check out even more information in a social media management tool like Hootsuite.

Reviewing your video engagement on its own is useful, but it can be helpful to zoom out a little, too. Check out average engagement rates by industry to see where you stand, or compare your performance to your top competitors.

You can also set up custom timeframes, switch between networks, like Instagram, Facebook, X, LinkedIn, and TikTok, and look up benchmarks for metrics like engagement rate, clicks, shares, and more.
And, if you need to present your results to your team or other stakeholders, you can easily download your comparison report as a PDF file.
If your engagement is low, you may need to read up on social video best practices to improve the quality, format, and overall strategy behind your videos.
Average watch time tells you how long people stick with your video and where you might be losing them.
“It’s one of the clearest signals of content quality and audience interest,” says Kwok, and it can guide everything from how you structure your videos to how long they should be.

“If you post a one-minute video and the average watch time is three seconds, it’s an indicator that the start of your video is missing a hook,” Kwok explains. “If you posted a three-second video and the average watch time is five seconds, that means the user watched the video more than once.”
Most platforms don’t use the exact label “average watch time,” but they do offer related metrics that can give you the same insight. Here’s what to look for:
Watch time: Total time your video or Reel was played (including replays).
3-second views: Number of times a viewer watched for at least 3 seconds.
1-minute views: Number of times someone watched to the 1-minute mark.
Average watch time: The average amount of time people spent watching your reel (watch time divided by initial views).
Watch time: Total time your reel was played, including replays.
Views: The number of times your reel started to play or replay.
Average watch time: The average amount of time spent watching your video per view, measured in seconds.
Total watch time: The total amount of time a video keeps playing on the screen, including any replays, while it remains visible to the viewer.
Views at 25%, 50%, 75%: Show how far viewers made it through your video.
Completions: Tracked when someone watches 97–100% of your video.
Completion rate: Completions divided by video impressions as a percentage.
Average watch time: The average amount of time people spent watching your video.
Video completion percentage: The number of times the video has been watched in full, as a percentage of viewers.
Estimated minutes watched: Total watch time across all views.
Average view duration: The average length of each view session.
Average view percentage: How much of each video is watched, on average.
Video completion rate is the percentage of viewers who watched your video all the way to the end. It’s calculated by dividing completed views by total views, then multiplying by 100.

Completion rate and average watch time answer different questions. Watch time tells you how much of your video got consumed on average. Completion rate tells you how many people stayed until the final frame. A 90-second explainer can post a healthy 45-second average watch time and still have a weak completion rate, which usually means the back half isn’t earning its length.

Thresholds vary by platform, so check the definition before you benchmark. LinkedIn, for example, counts a completion when someone watches 97 to 100% of your video. TikTok reports completion as a percentage of viewers who watched in full. YouTube frames the same idea as average percentage viewed rather than a binary completion.

Completion rate also feeds the algorithm. Videos that hold people to the end send a strong quality signal, which is part of why short-form content with tight edits tends to get pushed harder than longer cuts with slow middles. If your completion rate is sliding, the fix is usually trimming rather than adding.
Play rate is the percentage of people who saw your video and actually pressed play. Divide total plays by total impressions and multiply by 100.

Where view count measures how many people watched, play rate measures how persuasive your first impression was. A low play rate points to the elements that sit before the video starts: the thumbnail, the opening frame, the headline above it, or where the video is placed on the page. Those are all fixable without reshooting anything.

Play rate matters most in click-to-play environments, like YouTube, LinkedIn documents and articles, email, and video embedded on your website. On autoplay feeds such as TikTok, Reels, and Shorts, play rate loses meaning because the video starts on its own, so lean on retention and completion rate there instead. Not every platform surfaces play rate natively, so you may need to calculate it from plays and impressions yourself.

Click-through rate for video is the percentage of viewers who clicked your link or CTA. Divide clicks by total views, then multiply by 100. It’s the clearest measure of whether your video moved people from watching to doing.
CTR earns the most attention when your video has a job beyond awareness: paid campaigns, product launches, demo requests, or lead gen.

How you capture clicks differs by platform. YouTube gives you end screens, cards, and description links. TikTok routes most traffic through your bio link or a paid destination. Instagram relies on Stories links, bio links, and ad CTAs. LinkedIn lets you drop a link directly in the post copy. Because each path behaves differently, compare CTR within a platform rather than across them.

Shares are when viewers send your video to another user through DM or share it on their own page or story. And yes, while shares technically fall under engagement, they’re worth tracking as their own video metric.
Shares indicate that your video resonated with the viewer enough for them to share it with someone else. But shares are also an important metric from a consideration standpoint, according to Kwok.
“Shares are a form of word-of-mouth marketing,” Kwok says. “Users are more likely to pay attention to content that’s shared by their peers.”
Plus, Instagram’s been pretty open about the importance of creating shareable content. If your videos are getting more shares, they’re more likely to get priority in the recommendation algorithms.

TikTok works the same way. According to TikTok’s own recommendation documentation, shares sit alongside completion rate and rewatches as an interaction signal its recommendation system uses to decide how far a video travels, which is why a modest-reach video with heavy sharing can suddenly accelerate.
Saves are one of the strongest engagement signals you can earn on social video. When someone saves your content, they’re telling you it was useful, entertaining, or memorable enough to come back to.
That makes saves a great way to gauge what your audience actually finds valuable. Saving takes more effort than a quick like, which means a save is a bigger vote of confidence in your content.
Plus, platforms like Instagram and TikTok now treat saves as a key ranking signal in their recommendation systems.

Take a closer look at which Reels, TikToks, Shorts, and other social videos are saved most often. In practice, the heaviest savers tend to be reference-style content: step-by-step tutorials, templates, tool walkthroughs, and checklists people want to find again. If that’s where your saves cluster, make more of it and consider building a repeatable Reels series around the format.

Traffic source shows where your views are coming from, like search, feeds, profile visits, or external websites and shares. Knowing the traffic source can tell you where to spend more time and resources distributing your video content.
On YouTube, you’ll see if views came from search, suggested videos, or outside links. TikTok shows how many views came from the For You Page (FYP), your profile, or search.
“This indicates that the keywords used in the video were picked up by the TikTok algorithm, and your video was pushed to a wider audience,” says Kwok.

LinkedIn splits impressions by whether they came from the feed, your page or profile, or search and discovery surfaces. If most of your video impressions come from your own followers’ feeds, your distribution is capped by your follower base, which is a signal to lean harder on employee advocacy, hashtags, and paid amplification.

Use the pattern to set your distribution plan. Search-heavy sources reward keyword and caption work, while feed-heavy sources reward hooks and posting cadence. If you’re seeing strong numbers from external traffic sources, that means your content is reaching beyond your followers. And that’s always a good sign!
Conversion rate shows how many viewers took action after watching your video, whether that’s signing up, downloading, or buying. It’s the ultimate proof that your video content drove real results.

This metric is especially important when your video has a clear call-to-action (CTA). Think landing page videos, product explainers, or paid ads. If you’re asking viewers to do something, you need to know whether they actually followed through.
What counts as a conversion depends on your goal, but it could include:
Signing up for a webinar or event
To calculate conversion rate, divide the number of conversions by the number of video viewers (or clicks, if you’re using a link).

For paid and bottom-funnel video, platform-native tracking will give you cleaner attribution than link clicks alone. The Meta Pixel, TikTok Pixel, and LinkedIn Conversions API all let you tie on-site actions back to the video that drove them, which matters when your sales cycle runs longer than a single session.
A strong conversion rate means your message hits home. A weak one? Time to revisit your creative, CTA placement, or landing page experience.

Video retention rate tells you exactly how long viewers stick with your video, and when they lose interest. Unlike average watch time (which gives you a single number) or completion rate (which gives you a pass or fail), retention data reveals the precise moment viewers start to drop off.
Most platforms offer retention graphs that show:
If certain parts of your video get rewatched
How much of your video gets viewed on average
Knowing where drop-offs happen helps you answer the questions that actually shape your content:
This metric is especially important on platforms like Instagram, where seconds watched now carry significant weight.
Mosseri has confirmed that the algorithm pays close attention to total seconds viewed, not just completion percentage.

His logic: “We don’t want to penalize longer videos, which is why we look at not only the percentage of a video that was watched, but also the number of seconds. If you watched 10 seconds of a minute long video, that is just as many seconds as if it was 10 seconds of a 10 second video, so you won’t be penalized.”
Translation: Both completion rate and total seconds watched matter. Even if viewers don’t make it to the end, watching a chunk of a longer video still sends a positive signal to the algorithm.

How can you improve your social video metrics?
Improving your social video metrics comes down to understanding your audience and tweaking your strategy based on how they respond.
To get insider tips on what works, I asked Mariam (MJ) Ordubadi, Head of Marketing at Aequilibrium, for strategies to increase views, engagement, and retention.
Here are her top five tips:
Treat the first 3 seconds like prime real estate
Obsess over retention, not just views
Use AI creatively to drive results
1. Treat the first 3 seconds like prime real estate

Your video isn’t just competing with other content, it’s fighting against the scroll reflex, which is why Ordubadi’s team obsesses over hooks. As she puts it: “The first few seconds are make-or-break.”

One of her most reliable formulas? “The problem/solution hook: ‘Don’t have time to make dinner but need to finish your groceries? This hack will save you time and food rot.’ It works because it’s specific, urgent, and promises immediate value.”
But Ordubadi warns against clickbait: “The key is to stop the scroll without misleading your audience.”
Try this: Run your first 5 seconds through the “mute test.” If the visual alone doesn’t make someone unmute the video, it might be time to rework it.
Ordubadi’s team constantly analyzes how video length affects performance, and the takeaway is clear: there’s no universal “right” length, only the right length for the platform and goal.

“For TikTok, Reels, and Shorts, under 30 seconds still dominates for discovery,” Ordubadi notes, “But when the goal is education or conversion, we’ve had success with 2 to 3 minute videos on LinkedIn and YouTube, as long as every second delivers value.”
Ordubadi’s guiding principle? “I follow the ‘as short as possible, as long as necessary’ rule. No one wants to sit through fluff.”
The data backs this up: “Audience retention drops significantly after the 60-second mark unless your storytelling is really strong, so editing for pacing is just as important as length.”
Try this: Use YouTube’s retention graphs to identify “dead zones.” If 40% of viewers drop at 0:45, either cut that section or add a visual hook at 0:40 to pull them back in.
3. Obsess over retention, not just views
Retention tells you whether your content is actually landing. Which is why Ordubadi is more focused on what happens after the click.
“While view count is an attractive metric, I care more about average watch time and retention rate,” Ordubadi explains. “These tell me if the content is actually resonating.”

A view just shows that someone saw your video, maybe for a split second. Retention shows who stuck around, and for how long. Ordubadi adds, “I want to know what’s catching the audience’s attention and what makes them bounce.”
That said, engagement rate still matters: “I also note engagement rate (likes, comments, shares) to assess the overall community impact.”
Try this: Compare retention graphs across your last 5 videos. Look for patterns in the intros, pacing, or visuals that kept people watching. Then, repeat what works.
Some of Ordubadi’s biggest performance gains have come from a single insight: Creating content with repeat viewing in mind.
“Scripting for ‘loopable moments’ has transformed my approach,” Ordubadi says. “These are short videos that can be watched multiple times to fully grasp the message.”
Loopable content is especially effective with content like Instagram Reels and TikTok, where replay culture is baked into how people consume content.
“We saw this trend take off with brands like Duolingo, where looping drives higher watch time and retention,” Ordubadi notes.

It also opens the door to layered storytelling, a pattern that reflects broader shifts in social content consumption. Think: Pop culture nods, visual Easter eggs, or inside jokes meant for those “who are chronically online.”
Try this: Add one “rewatch trigger” (a blink-and-you-miss-it detail) in your next 5 videos and compare retention rates.
5. Use AI creatively to drive results
Ordubadi is closely watching the rise of AI-native video formats.
“There are these ‘talking document’ formats I’ve seen,” Ordubadi explains, “where a creator is breaking down a Google Sheet in real time with their face as a bubble in the corner.”

Ordubadi’s team is testing this style by repurposing internal strategy docs into social-friendly video explainers. “It’s performing particularly well on platforms where B2B audiences are looking for clarity and authenticity.”

More broadly, Ordubadi sees AI-powered content as a rising force in education and thought leadership: “There’s a huge wave in AI training hitting the scene from VR to social media. I see it as the next wave of educational content.”

If you’re scaling this kind of output, the AI assistant inside Hootsuite Social OS can help you draft captions, hooks, and variations for each platform so one video concept stretches across channels without starting from scratch each time.
Try this: Turn a behind-the-scenes doc, deck, or tool into a short, face-on video walkthrough. The key is blending value with relatability to earn trust, especially with professional audiences.

Video ROI is the return you get from video relative to what it cost to produce and distribute. It’s the number executives ask for, and the one most social teams struggle to produce because the inputs live in different systems.
Here’s the process in four steps:
Define the goal and the conversion. Decide what a win looks like before you publish: trial signups, demo requests, purchases, or qualified pipeline.
Add up the costs. Include production (crew, talent, editing, licensing), paid media spend, and any tooling or software allocated to the campaign.
Attribute the revenue. Use UTM parameters plus platform pixels or a conversions API so on-site actions trace back to the specific video.
Apply the formula. ROI equals revenue from video, minus video costs, divided by video costs, multiplied by 100.
A quick example: If a campaign cost $8,000 all in and drove $26,000 in attributed revenue, your ROI is (26,000 minus 8,000) divided by 8,000, multiplied by 100, which comes to 225%.

Not every video has a revenue job, and forcing one on awareness content will produce misleading numbers. For top-of-funnel work, report cost per thousand impressions, cost per view, or cost per engaged viewer instead, and keep hard ROI reserved for videos with a measurable conversion path. Being explicit about which videos are measured which way is what keeps the whole report credible.

What are the most important social video metrics for businesses?

The most important social video metrics for businesses are view count, play rate, average watch time, video completion rate, retention, engagement rate, shares, saves, click-through rate, traffic source, and conversion rate. Together, these metrics show whether your video content is reaching the right people, holding their attention, and driving real business impact.
What is a good video engagement rate across social platforms?

A good video engagement rate generally falls between 1% and 5%, though benchmarks vary by platform and industry. TikTok tends to see higher engagement rates than Instagram and YouTube, while X (Twitter) and Facebook usually trend lower.
How do video metrics differ across TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and LinkedIn?

Video metrics differ across TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and LinkedIn mostly in how each platform defines a “view.” TikTok counts a view at 1 second (or 3 seconds for videos 3 minutes and longer), Instagram counts a Reel view the moment it starts playing, YouTube counts a view at 30 seconds, and LinkedIn requires 2 seconds with at least 50% of the video on screen. That means the same piece of content can produce very different numbers depending on where it’s posted, so compare watch time and completion rate rather than raw views.
How do brands measure ROI from social video content?

Brands measure ROI from social video by subtracting video costs from the revenue attributed to video, dividing by those costs, and multiplying by 100. Costs include production, paid media, and tooling, while revenue is attributed using UTM links and platform pixels. The most accurate ROI picture combines hard conversions like sign-ups or purchases with softer signals like reach, retention, and engagement.
Social video views vs watch time: which metric matters more?

Watch time generally matters more than views because it shows whether viewers actually engaged with your content, not just whether the video started playing. That said, both metrics matter: views measure reach, while watch time measures depth. The strongest video strategies optimize for both.
What is play rate and why does it matter for video?

Play rate is the percentage of people who saw your video thumbnail or placement and actually pressed play, making it a direct measure of how compelling your video’s first impression is. It’s calculated by dividing plays by impressions and multiplying by 100. A low play rate usually points to a weak thumbnail, opening frame, or placement rather than a problem with the video itself.
What is a good video completion rate?

There’s no single universal benchmark for video completion rate, because it varies by platform, video length, and industry. Longer videos naturally see lower completion rates, so compare your results against videos of similar length on the same platform rather than against a single universal target. It also helps to check the platform’s own definition first. LinkedIn, for example, counts a completion at 97 to 100% watched.
How do you calculate click-through rate for social video?

Click-through rate for social video is calculated by dividing the number of clicks on your CTA or link by the total number of video views, then multiplying by 100. Because each platform routes clicks differently, through end screens, bio links, Stories links, or post copy, compare CTR within a single platform rather than across several.
What are the key metrics to track in social media marketing?

The key metrics to track in social media marketing depend on your goals, but the most universally important ones include engagement rate, reach, impressions, click-through rate, and conversion rate. For video specifically, add average watch time, completion rate, and retention, since those reveal whether people actually consumed the content.
What is the difference between video retention and video completion rate?

Video retention shows you where in the video viewers drop off, while video completion rate tells you the percentage of viewers who watched the entire video from start to finish. Retention is diagnostic and helps you fix specific moments, and completion rate is a summary signal that platforms use in their ranking systems.
